claims.feature: other: how the record is made
claims.claim: Le Guin says she worked out the kinship rules of the planet O by drawing charts with symbols and arrows.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Foreword to The Birthday of the World (2001)
claims.quote: I drew charts, with male and female symbols, and lines
claims.page: paragraph on A Fisherman of the Inland Sea

claims.claim: 'Mountain Ways' opens with an explicit note addressed to readers unfamiliar with the planet before the story starts.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Mountain Ways', excerpted on the author's official site
claims.quote: Note for readers unfamiliar with the planet O

claims.claim: The headnote sets out the four permitted relationships as a labelled list, each pairing given its own named term.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Mountain Ways' headnote, excerpted on the author's official site
claims.quote: The Morning woman and the Evening man (the "Morning marriage")

claims.claim: A Gethenian narrator explains the offworld convention for numbering years before stating her own.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Coming of Age in Karhide', excerpted on the author's official site
claims.quote: They call the year of some portentous event Year One

claims.claim: Two of the handbook's species entries end on a two-word status code.
claims.source: Le Guin, Rocannon's World (1966), opening handbook entry, quoted by Books & Boots
claims.page: prologue quotation, end of Species I-A entry

claims.claim: The handbook addresses its reader with a bare imperative telling him to note a social division.
claims.source: Le Guin, Rocannon's World (1966), opening handbook entry, quoted by Books & Boots
claims.quote: Note horizontal social cleavage into 2 pseudo-races

claims.claim: The survey entry sends the reader to numbered maps in a parenthesis inside the sentence.
claims.source: Le Guin, Rocannon's World (1966), second handbook entry, quoted by Books & Boots

claims.claim: The same entry cross-refers forward within the document rather than repeating the material.
claims.source: Le Guin, Rocannon's World (1966), second handbook entry, quoted by Books & Boots
claims.quote: see description of intelligent species below

claims.claim: The planetary entry gives the length of a year down to the second.
claims.source: Le Guin, Rocannon's World (1966), second handbook entry, quoted by Books & Boots

claims.claim: Le Guin's Foundation describes Tales from Earthsea as concluding with an account of the world's history, people, languages, literature and magic.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin Foundation, Tales from Earthsea book page
claims.quote: an account of Earthsea's history, people, languages, literature, and magic

claims.claim: Le Guin identifies the flat fantasy prose she is attacking as journalistic prose.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)

claims.claim: Le Guin says journalism deliberately suppresses the author's personality and sensibility to give an impression of objectivity.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)
claims.quote: the suppression of the author's personality and sensibility is deliberate

claims.claim: Le Guin says the journalistic technique is right for a newspaper but wrong for a novel and dead wrong for a fantasy.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)
claims.quote: This technique is right, for a newspaper.

claims.claim: Le Guin states flatly that speech expresses character, whether or not the speaker or author knows it.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)

claims.claim: Le Guin says most epics are in straightforward language, whether prose or verse, retaining the directness of their oral forebears.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)
claims.quote: Most epics are in straightforward language, whether prose or verse.

verdicts.trueWording: I drew charts, with male and female symbols, and lines
verdicts.note: Raw HTML of ursulakleguin.com foreword fetched with a browser UA (HTTP 200). Quote is verbatim in the paragraph beginning 'In the title story of the collection A Fisherman of the Inland Sea'; the sentence continues 'with arrows, very scientific.' The same paragraph supports the kinship limb: she says she spent systematic thought on the marriage and kinship customs of the people of O.

verdicts.trueWording: Note for readers unfamiliar with the planet O
verdicts.note: Raw page of the Birthday of the World excerpts fetched (HTTP 200). The line sits directly under the 'Mountain Ways' heading and before the story's first narrative paragraph ('Danro is the farthest farm...'), so the 'before the story starts' limb holds.

verdicts.trueWording: The Morning woman and the Evening man (the "Morning marriage")
verdicts.note: Verbatim on the same excerpts page. Lead-in line reads 'The expected relationships within each sedoretu are:' followed by four separate one-line items, each ending in a parenthesised name (Morning, Evening, Day, Night marriage); a fifth line then names the forbidden pairings. The claim's word 'permitted' is the page's 'expected', the only contrast on the page being 'forbidden'.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'the offworld convention' - the page attributes the Year One count to 'the Orgota, the Ekumen, and most other people', and the Orgota are a Gethenian nation, not offworlders
verdicts.trueWording: They call the year of some portentous event Year One
verdicts.note: Quote is verbatim. Byline on the page confirms the Gethenian narrator (Sov Thade Tage em Ereb, of Rer, in Karhide, on Gethen), and her own count is stated in the next sentence ('Here it's always Year One'), so the narrator and ordering limbs hold; only the 'offworld' attribution overreaches, since Orgoreyn is on Gethen.

verdicts.trueWording: Status C-Prime; the Fua entry closes Status E-Query
verdicts.note: astrofella.wordpress.com fetched raw (HTTP 200, 166 KB). The blog quotes the Pocket Guide prologue in full: entry I-A ends 'Status C-Prime.' and entry I-B ends 'Status E-Query.'; the Species II (Liuar) entry carries no status. So exactly two of the three species entries close on a two-word status code.

verdicts.trueWording: Note horizontal social cleavage into 2 pseudo-races
verdicts.note: Verbatim inside the Species II (Liuar) entry on the same page, a bare imperative followed by the two named pseudo-races (Olgyior 'midmen', Angyar 'lords'). The reader-addressing limb rests on the imperative itself; the page assigns the reader no gender.
Verbatim in the second handbook quotation, First Geographical Survey entry, as a parenthesis inside the sentence about the major landmasses being surveyed by air.

Verbatim in the same First Geographical Survey entry, closing the sentence about landings and HILF contacts on East and Northwest Continents. 'below' is the document's own forward pointer, and the entry gives no species description of its own.
Verbatim in the physical-description block of the second handbook quotation, alongside Rotation, mean distance and obliquity. Revolution is the orbital year, given to the second.

verdicts.trueWording: an account of Earthsea's history, people, languages, literature, and magic
verdicts.note: ursulakleguin.com/tales-from-earthsea fetched raw (HTTP 200). The book description reads 'Concluding with with an account of...' (the doubled 'with' is the page's own typo); the footer identifies the site as The Ursula K. Le Guin Foundation, supporting the attribution limb.

PDF fetched (HTTP 200, 347 KB, 8 pages) and text extracted with pdftotext -layout; the phrase is on page 8, confirming the cited location. The paragraph two above it names 'the kind of writing I am attacking, the Poughkeepsie style of fantasy' and calls it flat and only apparently plain, which supports the 'flat fantasy prose she is attacking' limb.

verdicts.trueWording: the suppression of the author's personality and sensibility is deliberate
verdicts.note: Page 8 of the PDF, immediately after 'In journalism,'; the following sentence states that the goal is an impression of objectivity, supporting that limb.

verdicts.trueWording: This technique is right, for a newspaper.
verdicts.note: Page 8 of the PDF. The sentence continues that it is wrong for a novel and dead wrong for a fantasy, so all three limbs of the claim are on the page.
Page 4 of the PDF, confirming the cited page. The next sentence adds that it does so whether or not the speaker or the author knows it, which is the claim's second limb.

verdicts.trueWording: Most epics are in straightforward language, whether prose or verse.
verdicts.note: Page 8 of the PDF. The next sentence says they retain the directness of their oral forebears, supporting the claim's second limb; the paragraph goes on to Homer, Roland and the sagas.
